newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL UNDERWEIGHTS MANILA BANKS.
newsitem.headline: DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL UNDERWEIGHTS MANILA BANKS.

text.p: Philippine listed banks are likely to post slower growth in the medium-term following the de facto devaluation of the peso, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said in a report in which it downgraded the sector to "underweight" from "neutral."
Morgan Grenfell banking analyst Michaelangelo Oyson said a weaker peso and high interest rates would put pressure on the asset quality of banks, and consequently, their growth potential.

The report for August, made available to Reuters on Monday, said: "The sector is expected to underperform and current valuations are unattractive. We recommend an underweight on the sector. Lower ratings are deserved because of asset quality concerns and a slowdown in EPS growth."

Oyson said the recent de facto peso devaluation will trigger a surge in loan defaults because of foreign exchange losses and higher principal and interest payments, especially from foreign currency and real estate-related loans.
Loan delinquencies, which stood at 1.9 percent of the total portfolio in 1996, were expected to worsen to 2.3 percent in 1998, and 2.7 percent in 1999.

Oyson said as much as 20 percent of the dollar borrowers do not have dollar revenues. Dollar loans have increased to 25 percent of the total loan portfolio as of the first quarter of the year from 19 percent in 1995 and 16 percent in 1992.
Deteriorating land values, due to an impending housing and office space glut, will further put pressure on the banks' bottom line. Property loans were a major source of growth in the past two years.
As a result, banks would be forced to beef up their loan loss provisions, which have declined to 1.5 percent from 3.3 percent in 1993.

Oyson said fee-based income would not compensate for the slowdown in traditional banking. "Fee income will not be substantial even if foreign exchange profits expand, as few deals are in the pipeline and operating expenses keep mounting due to automation and wage hikes."

"We are downgrading our sector view from neutral to underweight after a cut in our 1998 sector EPS growth forecast from 26 percent to 15 percent and a modest 10 percent year-on-year growth in 1999," Oyson said.
"We expect another de-rating as investors focus on the combination of deteriorating asset and earnings quality. Despite seemingly cheap valuations, we still expect a further de-rating," he added.

Oyson recommended a hold on Metropolitan Bank and Trust Co on a three-month basis and underweight for the next 12 months; while sell on Equitable Bank for the next three months and underweight over the next 12 months.
Bank of the Philippine Islands and Philippine National Bank were hold/neutral; while Union Bank of the Philippines and Security Bank Corp were hold/underweight.
Philippine Commercial International Bank was sell/neutral.
Far East Bank and Trust Co was the only buy/overweight in the list due to its oversold position, only 11 times its 1997 projected earnings ratio.
